content: Occlusion in dentistry refers to the contact between teeth. More specifically, it describes the relationship between the maxillary (upper) and mandibular (lower) teeth when they come into contact, such as during chewing or when the jaw is at rest. Malocclusion, commonly referred to as a bad bite, is the misalignment of teeth and jaws. This condition can lead to various health and dental issues. Static occlusion describes the contact between teeth when the jaw is closed and stationary, whereas dynamic occlusion refers to the contact between teeth when the jaw is in motion, such as during chewing. Centric occlusion is the position of the teeth when the jaw is closed, and the teeth are in maximum intercuspation, meaning they fit together as tightly as possible. This is also known as a person’s habitual bite, bite of convenience, or intercuspal position (ICP). Centric relation, on the other hand, is a specific relationship between the upper and lower jaws and should not be confused with centric occlusion. Malocclusion can result in a range of problems affecting not only the teeth but also the gums, temporomandibular joint (TMJ), and jaw muscles. Teeth, fillings, and crowns may wear down, break, or become loose, and teeth may become tender or painful. Receding gums can be worsened by an improper bite. TMJ disorders, broadly referred to as temporomandibular joint syndrome, can manifest as clicking, grinding, or pain in the jaw joint, ringing or buzzing in the ears, and difficulty opening or closing the mouth. If the jaw is misaligned, the jaw muscles may need to exert extra effort, leading to fatigue or muscle spasms. This can further result in headaches or migraines, pain around the eyes or sinuses, and discomfort in the neck, shoulders, or even the back. If left untreated, severe malocclusion can lead to occlusal trauma, which can cause significant damage to the teeth and surrounding structures. Treatments for occlusal problems vary and may include tooth adjustments, replacement of missing teeth, temporary medication, a diet of softer foods, or relaxation therapy to address stress-related clenching. Fixed appliances, such as orthodontic braces, may be used to correct occlusion, while removable appliances, known as occlusal splints, can also be employed for adjustments and other therapeutic purposes.
